title: Specification · Agent-friendly engineering · Failure modes
description: Turn an ambiguous maintenance request into observable behaviour, executable feedback and a diagnosis that explains how a failed run can be repaired.

sections.title: Two correct answers to the wrong question

blocks.body:
Our retry helper now has a clear convention: a retry count of two permits an initial attempt and two further attempts. Imagine that the next issue simply says, “Make retries more robust.” One agent increases the limit. Another adds a delay. A third retries every exception instead of only timeouts. Each patch makes sense under some interpretation of “robust”. Those interpretations disagree about what the program should do.

We can picture the request as a region containing many possible programs. Every additional requirement cuts away some of that region. “Keep the public API unchanged” excludes patches that rename the argument. “Do not retry authentication failures” excludes patches that repeat every failed operation. Eventually the remaining programs share the behaviour we care about, even though their internal code may differ.

That is the useful job of a specification: remove uncertainty about the result while leaving room to discover a good implementation. A line-by-line recipe can remove freedom without resolving the important ambiguity. “Add a loop around the call” still says nothing about which failures belong inside that loop.

There is another reason to settle the contract early. Once a plausible patch exists, it becomes easy to explain why that particular patch was the intention all along. Writing down a few observable expectations before editing gives us something stable against which to judge the result. We can revise those expectations when we learn more, but the revision should be visible rather than silently following whatever the implementation happens to do.

Sometimes the necessary decision already exists in documentation or established callers. Then the task is to find it. Sometimes the sources conflict. Then investigation has exposed a product decision, and further code generation cannot settle it. A useful agent distinguishes these situations: missing evidence calls for a search; genuinely unspecified behaviour calls for a decision by whoever owns that behaviour.

sections.title: Make the difference visible at the boundary

blocks.body:
For this fictional helper, suppose we agree on a particular change. Keep the existing argument meaning: zero retries still makes one initial call, and two retries permits at most three calls. Retry only errors recognised by the existing timeout classifier. Keep the current delay policy, with each wait capped at one second. Return immediately on success. If every permitted attempt times out, propagate the first timeout object unchanged. If any attempt fails with a different error, propagate that error immediately.

The last two sentences are deliberately separate. Consider a timeout followed by an authentication error. “Return the original error” could mean returning the timeout, concealing the authentication failure. Our contract instead gives the terminal, non-timeout error precedence. The first-timeout rule applies only when the attempt budget is exhausted entirely by timeouts. This is a choice for this helper, not a universal retry policy.

Now we can make the behaviour visible as a sequence of events. With two retries available:

```text
timeout A → success V           returns V after 2 calls
timeout A → timeout B → timeout C
                               throws A after 3 calls
timeout A → authentication E    throws E after 2 calls
authentication E               throws E after 1 call
```

Notice how much the third sequence contributes. A test of immediate authentication failure could pass even if a bug swallowed every non-timeout error that occurred after the first timeout. The mixed sequence distinguishes two implementations that the simpler cases cannot tell apart.

The same reasoning exposes a timing boundary. A wait belongs between a retryable failure and an actual next attempt. There should be no wait after success, after a terminal error, or after the last permitted timeout. Counting calls alone cannot reveal an unnecessary final delay; observing both calls and scheduled waits can.

We have moved from an adjective to traces that a caller could distinguish. The implementation may use a loop, recursion or an existing utility. Those choices are secondary unless the repository imposes another constraint. The observable result is what connects the request, the implementation and the evidence.

blocks.question: With two retries available, the first call times out and the second fails authentication. How many calls and waits should this contract produce?
blocks.answer: Two calls and one wait. The timeout permits another attempt, so there is one intervening wait. The authentication error is terminal: propagate that error immediately, without a third call or another wait.

sections.title: The boundary around a small change

blocks.body:
A behavioural contract does not describe the whole assignment. Our helper might be correct while the patch also changes every caller, replaces the logging system and updates unrelated dependencies. Those changes create extra review work and extra ways for something to break. We therefore need a boundary around the work as well as a boundary around the function.

Here, preserving the API and the existing timeout classifier keeps the change local. Introducing a new backoff algorithm is outside the request. So is widening the set of operations that are retried. These exclusions matter because repeating an operation can have effects beyond the helper: a caller may submit a payment or create a resource. Whether such repetition is safe depends on the surrounding operation and its guarantees. Fixing the counter does not establish those guarantees. The [AWS Builders’ Library discussion of idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/) explores why repeated requests need an explicit contract for their effects.

A non-goal is most useful when it rules out a tempting expansion. Listing every conceivable thing the agent must never do makes the brief harder to read without clarifying the task. A small set of relevant constraints, placed where they affect a decision, usually communicates more.

The stopping point also needs meaning. “Keep improving until confident” has no observable end. For this change, we can finish when the agreed traces are checked against the final patch, the relevant caller remains compatible, and the diff stays within scope. If an integration environment is unavailable, that limitation changes what can be claimed. It may still be possible to deliver a locally verified patch for review; it is not possible to turn the unavailable environment into evidence by describing it confidently.

These boundaries leave the agent substantial freedom: where to investigate, how to organise the implementation and which additional checks would expose a plausible mistake. We are specifying what a successful handoff contains, rather than prescribing every action on the way there.

sections.title: Give the investigation something useful to push against

blocks.body:
Now imagine handing that brief to an agent in a repository with three obsolete test commands and two files named retry, one generated from the other. The behavioural uncertainty is gone, but the agent still has to discover how to ask the repository a useful question. Every false start consumes attention that could have gone into the actual bug.

Repository structure can remove that friction. A recognisable source directory tells the agent where changes belong. A nearby test shows how the helper is called. A short, accurate command tells it how to execute that test. These are useful to a new human colleague for the same reason: they connect an intention to an action whose result can be interpreted.

For the retry helper, the most helpful affordance might be a controllable operation that returns a programmed sequence of outcomes. Give it timeout A, timeout B and success V, and it records each call. Replace real waiting with an injectable clock or delay function, and the test can inspect scheduled delays without sleeping through them. Now a trace that was previously a thought experiment becomes a repeatable observation.

That substitution has a boundary of its own. A fake delay can show that the helper requests the right wait at the right point. It does not prove that the real timer or the external service behaves correctly. The focused test answers a narrow question quickly; integration checks answer different questions. Confusing those roles either makes every small test slow and fragile or makes a tiny test appear to establish far too much.

Useful failures preserve the distinction we are trying to learn. “Expected three calls, observed four” points toward the attempt boundary. “Cannot import the timeout fixture” says the experiment never reached that boundary. Both commands may exit with an error, but their meaning is different. A harness that returns the actual assertion, the command and the relevant output gives the next model call a chance to respond to that difference.

A test like this can run itself, produce a result and hand that result back into the loop; a paragraph of written guidance cannot. This is why a repository full of instructions can still be difficult to work in. Prose about diligence cannot replace a test that can run. When a convention can be expressed in a formatter, a type or a focused check, that executable feedback often does more than repeating the convention in another document. Keep written guidance for the context and decisions those tools cannot express.

data.title: A test turns a distinction into feedback
data.caption: The contract supplies an expected trace. The implementation supplies an observed trace. Comparing them can guide a change; an experiment that never runs supplies neither a pass nor a behavioural failure.

sections.title: Find where the evidence and the action parted company

blocks.body:
Suppose the resulting patch changes the delay but leaves the extra attempt untouched. The final answer looks like a reasoning mistake. Before concluding that the model needs a stronger warning, reconstruct the path that produced it.

If the request only said “robust”, the run may have solved a different specification. If the exact assertion existed but never entered the context, the missing fact belongs to the input path. If the agent requested the right test but a missing dependency prevented execution, the environment blocked the observation. If it saw the contract and the trace, yet concluded that four calls were permitted, reasoning is the more plausible place to investigate. If an irrelevant green suite was presented as proof, the acceptance process also failed.

These categories describe possible causes, not mutually exclusive labels. A confusing brief and a weak test can cooperate to produce a polished wrong answer. Start with the earliest divergence you can actually establish, while retaining later failures that would still need repair. A failed test launch does not prove that the patch is correct or incorrect; it establishes that this run did not obtain that evidence.

The diagnosis should predict what a repair will change. If the missing assertion is the problem, supplying it should let the agent identify the attempt-count mismatch. If the wrong package was tested, fixing the working directory should expose the relevant failure. If adequate evidence was misread, asking for the sequence of counter values may reveal the precise step where the interpretation goes wrong.

Keep the original run, then change one relevant condition when practical. Replacing the model, rewriting the task and repairing the environment at once may produce a better result, but it leaves the explanation unresolved. Even a targeted change followed by success is only evidence for a diagnosis: outputs vary, and another run may differ. Repeat the comparison if you need to establish reliability rather than recover this one task.

sections.title: Let a failed run teach you something specific

blocks.body:
Take a small maintenance task with an observable result. It can be the retry helper, or a real failure you can reproduce safely in a disposable checkout. Keep the original request and the evidence the agent actually received. You are looking for the first point where the intended investigation and the recorded run diverge.

If the agent succeeds, there is no need to manufacture a dramatic failure. Inspect which observation made success possible. Then consider what would happen if that observation were absent or misleading. If it fails, choose a repair that makes a prediction you can check: the right test will execute, a missing distinction will become visible, or an incorrect trace will be corrected.

The interesting output is a causal account of the run. “The second answer was better” is an observation; “the second answer used the previously missing attempt-count assertion, and its patch now passes that regression case” explains more. Keep any remaining uncertainty visible. One repaired run tells us how a failure might be prevented. The next chapter asks how to find out whether that improvement survives across a useful sample of work.

data.title: Lab 3 · Investigate one run
data.brief: Use a small maintenance task to explain which observation or missing condition shaped the result. A successful run is useful evidence too.
steps: Preserve the request, starting state and observations from one run.
Locate a specific divergence, or identify the observation that enabled success.
Predict the effect of changing one relevant condition, then try it in an isolated workspace.
Compare the recorded behaviour and explain what the experiment did and did not establish.
deliverables: A short trace connecting the request, evidence and action
A targeted change with a prediction and observed result
data.review: The explanation should connect the changed condition to an observable difference. An unchanged outcome or an inconclusive experiment is valid if its limits are explained.

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library: making retries safe with idempotent APIs

heading: How do you make the intended result unambiguous?
lead: A small retry change can hide several different definitions of correct. Follow those differences until they become observable, then give the agent a way to test them and learn from a miss.
outcomes: Specify behaviour and scope without prescribing the implementation.
Build feedback that distinguishes a code defect from a failed experiment.
Use a recorded run to form and test a targeted recovery hypothesis.
